title: The Origins of Antisemitism
author: Sam Venis
content:
![The Origins of
Antisemitism](https://storage.ghost.io/c/65/af/65afbdb5-30bf-4286-acc4-9535069adb42/content/images/2026/09/IMG_4500-1.jpg)

In 1944, when Hannah Arendt sat down to compose the notes for what would
become _The Origins of Totalitarianism_ , not two years had passed since news
of the Nazi death camps had reached America. American troops were on their way
to the beaches of Normandy to sledgehammer into Europe, but the streets of
Paris were still under German control. After moving to Manhattan's Upper West
Side in 1941, Arendt had begun working for a German-Jewish weekly called
_Aufbau_ , for which she wrote many of the essays that would become _The_
_Origins_. As she described it, the project sought to explain a vague but
widely shared agreement that "the essential structure of all civilizations is
at a breaking point." More specifically, Arendt set out to answer how death
camps and a World War could be set in motion by "so small (and, in world
politics, so unimportant) a phenomenon as the Jewish question."

In order to do this, Arendt addressed two theses on the source of
antisemitism, both of them held widely among the Jewish organizations lobbying
Washington for European intervention, and equally among the impoverished
emigrant Jews who were scrambling to rebuild their lives in the new world.

The first was the thesis of "eternal antisemitism": the idea that "mankind has
insisted on murdering Jews for more than two thousand years" in a historical
chain reaching back to the sack of Jerusalem, the blood libels, and the
Crusades. The second thesis, which she called the scapegoat theory, held that
Jews had become the sacrificial lamb of totalitarian fascism almost by
accident: that when a machinery of violence like the Nazis' spins out of
control, anyone could become the target of the bloody cleansing.

> "Arendt argued that both theories were wrong."

Arendt argued that both theories were wrong--indeed, they were facile ways for
Jews to "escape the seriousness of antisemitism" by waving away the political
conditions of European society with psychological explanations that veered
into the mystical. With regard to the scapegoat theory, she noted that before
the Jews were the victims of Nazi terror, they were the center of Nazi
ideology, and an ideology that must convince people to mobilize cannot choose
its victims arbitrarily. As for "eternal antisemitism," she didn't deny the
long history of Jew hatred among the peoples of Europe, but she argued that
modern antisemitism, of the variety produced by the Nazis, was categorically
different from what had come before. _The Origins of Totalitarianism_
presented her alternative view.
